paper.title: How Java's Floating-Point Hurts Everyone Everywhere
paper.venue: work-in-progress note, University of California, Berkeley (version of 30 July 2004); invited talk, ACM 1998 Workshop on Java for High-Performance Network Computing
paper.text_read: https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~wkahan/JAVAhurt.pdf (fetched 2026-11-19; the program for A(x) on page 27-28, the f(x) example on page 35 and example 7 on pages 51-54 taken from the text)

program.how: written for ounce-core from the programs and data in the paper; exp, sin, tan are written here (no libm); double-double arithmetic (Knuth/Dekker algorithms, written here) gives the high-precision value; no third-party code
program.target: static freestanding aarch64 Linux ELF, run with `ounce-core run-elf --cpu=tier3`; the same source also builds natively (-DHOST) for a bit-for-bit comparison

claims_checked: A(x) = (x-1)/(exp(x-1)-1) computed in binary32 by the paper's program (Y = X-1; Z = EXP(Y); if Z != 1 then Z = Y/(Z-1)), with x within 20000 ulps of 1 on both sides: the worst error is 2895.8 ulps (the paper: 'about +-2900 = 2^11.5 ULPs', read from its plot), below 2^12 ulps, so less than half of the 24 bits are lost

nearest point on a line (example 7): with every operation in float the first formula gives z = [1, 1, -1] as the paper says; with subexpressions in double and one rounding to float it gives the correctly rounded [1/3, 2/3, -4/3] (as floats)

f(x) = (tan(sin x) - sin(tan x))/x^7 at x = 0.0200000 equals 0.0333486813 to the printed 9 significant digits (double-double, about 32 digits), while plain double arithmetic gives 0.0333446378 (relative error 1.2e-4), so double precision does not suffice

expected_values_source.what: numbers and data printed in the paper
expected_values_source.tolerance: the 2900-ulp figure is read from a plot, so a window 2500..3300 ulps was fixed before the first run (the measured 2895.8 lies inside); z and f(x) digits are compared exactly (f(x) as printed, rounded or truncated at 9 digits)

observations: the paper also prints z2 = [1.000000054, 1.000000054, -1.500000148] for its second formula in float; those numbers are not binary32 values (the spacing of floats near 1 is 1.2e-7), so they cannot come from an all-float computation and are not reproduced; my all-float evaluation of the second formula gives [1, 1, -1.5]
the paper's claim 'at least 19 sig. dec. must be carried' for f(x) is not tested; only that double is insufficient and double-double reproduces the printed value
negative_control: built with -DNEG_NOROUND (exp(y) replaced by 1 + y), the worst error of the A(x) program becomes 19992 ulps, the two A(x) checks fail and the program exits 1
not_checked: the paper's other seven nearest-point examples, its complex-arithmetic and Java-language arguments, and its rounding-mode examples
the claim that A(x) is provably accurate to half the bits in general (only measured on 40001 floats near 1), and the exact value 2900 (only the stated window)
the 19-digit claim for f(x) and arithmetic in other precisions
Tier-4 and native ARM64 execution (the native comparison here is x86-64)
what_a_pass_means: ounce-core's binary32 and double arithmetic reproduce three numerical examples of the paper (the error bound of A(x), the all-float result of the line example and the printed value of f(x)). It does not show the paper's arguments about Java.
